latin.384: GAR. Denique falsum assumit, qui supponit parentum crimen nunquam nascituris, aut nepotibus imputari: cum exempla in contrarium suppetant bene multa: Infamia enim, & honorum privatio, & exilium etiam in nepotes perduellium non infrequentur descendunt. Quod & Scripturae exempla postea manifestum facient.
latin.385: PLAC. Si parentum crimen nascituris & nepotibus imputatur a Deo, id fit, quia illud crimen in nascituris & nepotibus etiam locum habet, maiorum traditiones & mores imitantibus, aut probantibus. Sic peccatum Jeroboami, eo mortuo, in decem tribubus permansit, & peccatum Judaeorum, qui Dominum gloriae crucifixerunt, eorum posteri hodie probant, & in seipsis fovent ac conservant.
latin.386: Nec unquam reperietur Deum Judicem, aut suo judicio fecisse peccatorem eum, qui alioqui non fuisset peccator, aut sententia sua privasse aliquem justitia inhaerente, aut punivisse aliquem, in quo non esset peccatum, quod illam poenam mereretur. Si quando nulla habita ratione peccati, pro summa sua in creaturas potestate, aliquem affligi permittit, ut Jobum, & caecum illum cuius historia narratur Joh. 9. id non facit ut judex, nec ut justitiae satisfiat, nec ut legis comminatio adimpleatur, sed ut supremus creaturae suae Dominus, qui ea uti potest pro suo arbitrio ad gloriam suam, ad Ecclesiae aedificationem, ad confusionem hostium suorum, ad probationem illius qui sic affligitur.
latin.387: Certe eiusmodi imputatione ut bonis illis priventur nihil opus est. Sufficit enim ad id, parentem quacumque demum ratione, vel bellica clade, vel Domini injustitia, vel vicini iniuria, vel aliqua alia ratione sine ullo infidelitatis crimine Aulicum amittere, aut etiam vendere, & pecuniam consumere: iisdem illis bonis privabuntur haeredes absque ulla infidelitatis imputatione, aut judicis sententia, hac sola de causa, quoniam nemo dat quod non habet. Filii haeredes sunt bonorum paternorum. Quae autem pater vel amisit, vel vendidit in bonis paternis non amplius sunt. Quod si humanus judex paternum crimen filiis imputat, num idem Deus facere censendus est? Utrum aequius est nostras de Dei justitia cogitationes ad legum humanarum normam exigere, quam ad ipsius Dei legem? non arbitror. Audi legem Dei. Deut. 24. 16. Ne morte afficiuntor patres pro filiis, ne filii morte afficiuntor pro patribus: quisque propter peccatum suum afficiuntor morte.
latin.388: Ac ne crimen infidelitatis, vel laesae majestatis excipias, obstat Scriptura, 2. Chr. 25. 3. Amazia interfecit servos suos qui percusserant Regem patrem suum: filios vero eorum non affecit morte: sed fecit sicut scriptum est in lege praecepisse Jehovam dicendo, ne moriuntor patres pro filiis & filii ne moriuntor pro patribus, sed quisque propter peccatum suum moriuntor. Quid quod ipse Deus vindicans suam justitiam a Judaeorum calumniis quid sit nobis de ea sentiendum praescripsit? Anima, inquit, quae peccat ipsa morietur. Filius non feret iniquitatem patris, pater non feret iniquitatem filii &c.
latin.389: GAR. Atqui responsuris illud ante omnia clare fuerat explicandum, putentne in eiusmodi magistratuum judiciis aliquid injustum aut crudele designari, quod secus fieri oportuerit, & cuius nomine in foro conscientiae justa possint accusatione percelli. Nam si justa sunt ea Judicum sententiae, non dubium est quin suam apud Deum approbationem habeant, qui quae justa sunt & bona non potest non approbare cum fiunt. Quae vero justa & bona & sancta sunt, apud homines recte sentientes, cur tanquam absurda, & immania, & injustitia plena traducantur, cum a Deo fieri dicuntur? PLAC. Aut bona est mea responsio, aut mala. Si bona, cur eam non admisit Vir doctus? Si mala, debuit eius vitium ostendere, non aliam mihi respondendi rationem praescribere. Deinde illa ipsa respondendi ratio quam exigit potest in eum retorqueri: nam vel justae sunt eiusmodi judicum sententiae, vel injustae. Si justae, demonstrare debuit earum justitiam, vel Scripturae aliquo testimonio, vel necessaria & evidenti ratione, unde constet similibus Deum delectari sententiis.

pass_a.384: GAR's last: it is false to suppose parents' crime is never imputed to the yet-unborn or to grandsons. Many contrary examples stand ready—infamy, loss of honors, and exile often descend even on traitors' grandsons—and Scripture's examples will make that plain later.
pass_a.385: Placeus: if God imputes parents' crime to the unborn and to grandsons, it is because that crime also has place in them as they imitate or approve ancestors' traditions and manners. So Jeroboam's sin remained in the ten tribes after his death, and the Jews who crucified the Lord of glory have posterity who still approve and foster that sin in themselves.
pass_a.386: Never will God as Judge be found to have made a sinner of one who otherwise would not have been, or by sentence to have stripped inhering justice, or to have punished where no deserving sin was. When without regard to sin he permits affliction by supreme power over creatures—as Job, or the blind man in John 9—he acts not as judge for justice or law's threat, but as supreme Lord using the creature for glory, the Church's building-up, enemies' confusion, and the afflicted's proving.
pass_a.387: No such imputation is needed for heirs to lose those goods. A parent may lose or sell them by war, a lord's injustice, a neighbor's injury, or other cause without unfaithfulness—and heirs are stripped without imputing unfaithfulness or a judge's sentence, simply because no one gives what he does not have. Sons inherit paternal goods; what father lost or sold is gone. If a human judge imputes the father's crime to sons, must God do the same? Better measure God's justice by his own law than by human laws. Hear Deut. 24:16: each dies for his own sin, not fathers for sons or sons for fathers.
pass_a.388: Lest unfaithfulness or lese-majesty be excepted, 2 Chr. 25:3 stands: Amaziah killed the servants who struck his father the King, but not their sons, doing as Jehovah commanded—fathers not dying for sons nor sons for fathers, each for his own sin. God himself, vindicating his justice from Jewish calumnies, prescribed what to think: the soul that sins shall die; the son shall not bear the father's iniquity, nor the father the son's.
pass_a.389: GAR presses first that respondents must say plainly whether in such magistrates' judgments anything unjust or cruel is marked which ought to have been done otherwise, and for which they could be justly accused in conscience. If those judges' sentences are just, God who cannot but approve what is just and good must approve them when done; why then are the same acts traduced as absurd, monstrous, and full of injustice when said to be done by God among men who think rightly? Placeus answers: either his reply is good—why did the learned man not admit it?—or bad—he ought to show the fault, not prescribe another path of answering. That demanded path turns back on the objector: those sentences are just or unjust; if just, he must demonstrate their justice by Scripture testimony or by necessary evident reason that God delights in like sentences. Tip before human testimony / power-vs-justice deepen.

384: GAR. Finally, he assumes something false who supposes that parents' crime is never imputed to those yet to be born, or to grandsons: seeing that examples to the contrary are ready in plenty. For infamy, and deprivation of honors, and exile not infrequently descend even upon the grandsons of traitors. Which Scripture's examples will afterward also make plain.
385: PLAC. If parents' crime is imputed by God to those yet to be born and to grandsons, that is done because that crime also has place in those yet to be born and in grandsons, imitating or approving the traditions and manners of their ancestors. So Jeroboam's sin, he being dead, remained in the ten tribes, and the sin of the Jews who crucified the Lord of glory their posterity today approve, and foster and conserve in themselves.
386: Nor will it ever be found that God as Judge, or by his judgment, made him a sinner who otherwise would not have been a sinner, or by his sentence stripped anyone of inhering justice, or punished anyone in whom there was not a sin that deserved that penalty. If sometimes, no account being taken of sin, by his supreme power over creatures he permits someone to be afflicted—as Job, and that blind man whose history is told in John 9—he does that not as judge, nor that justice be satisfied, nor that the law's threat be fulfilled, but as supreme Lord of his creature, who can use it at his pleasure for his glory, for the Church's edification, for the confusion of his enemies, for the proving of him who is so afflicted.
387: Certainly there is no need of such an imputation for them to be deprived of those goods. For it is enough to that end that the parent, by whatever reason at last—by war's disaster, or a lord's injustice, or a neighbor's injury, or some other reason without any crime of unfaithfulness—lose as Courtier, or even sell, and spend the money: the heirs will be deprived of those same goods without any imputation of unfaithfulness, or a judge's sentence, for this sole cause—that no one gives what he does not have. Sons are heirs of the paternal goods. But what the father either lost or sold is no longer among the paternal goods. But if a human judge imputes the father's crime to the sons, is God to be thought to do the same? Is it fairer to measure our thoughts of God's justice by the norm of human laws than by God's own law? I do not think so. Hear God's law. Deut. 24:16. Fathers shall not be put to death for sons, nor sons put to death for fathers: each shall be put to death for his own sin.
388: And lest you except the crime of unfaithfulness or of lese-majesty, Scripture stands in the way, 2 Chr. 25:3. Amaziah killed his servants who had struck the King his father: but their sons he did not put to death: but he did as it is written in the law that Jehovah commanded, saying, fathers shall not die for sons and sons shall not die for fathers, but each shall die for his own sin. What of this—that God himself, vindicating his justice from the Jews' calumnies, prescribed what we ought to think of it? The soul, he says, that sins, it shall die. The son shall not bear the father's iniquity, the father shall not bear the son's iniquity, &c.
389: GAR. But for those about to answer, that ought first of all to have been clearly explained—whether they think in such magistrates' judgments anything unjust or cruel is designated which ought to have been done otherwise, and on account of which they can be struck with just accusation in the forum of conscience. For if those Judges' sentences are just, there is no doubt they have their approval with God, who cannot but approve what is just and good when it is done. But what is just and good and holy among men who think rightly—why is it traduced as absurd and monstrous and full of injustice when it is said to be done by God? PLAC. Either my reply is good, or bad. If good, why did the learned man not admit it? If bad, he ought to have shown its fault, not prescribe me another way of answering. Then that very way of answering which he demands can be turned back on him: for either such judges' sentences are just, or unjust. If just, he ought to have demonstrated their justice, either by some testimony of Scripture, or by a necessary and evident reason, whence it would be clear that God delights in like sentences.
